_what: Section 07: the argument over Planet Nine, year by year, in three lanes. Arguments for a planet on the left, arguments against one on the right, and the data (new objects, searches, surveys) down the middle, branching toward the side its authors say it favours.
_caution: 'lane' and 'branch' are our editorial reading of what each paper does to the argument, like 'stance' in papers.json. Say so on the site.
Entries with a 'doi' take their title, authors, citation count and links from papers.json; the 'text' here is a plain-language retelling of that paper's abstract-checked summary.
'excluded' percentages are the fractions of the predicted parameter space a null search ruled out, quoted from the paper's abstract.

Photos and figures are Wikimedia Commons files. scripts/fetch_portraits.py downloads them, crops them, and fills in 'credit', 'license' and 'source' from the Commons API, so nothing about licensing is typed by hand.
Where no freely licensed portrait exists, the card shows the instrument or institution behind the work, or a monogram.
'future' entries describe searches that are under way or proposed. They are not findings.

_lanes.support: argues the pattern is real and a planet is the best explanation
_lanes.against: argues the pattern is a selection effect, or that something other than a planet explains it
_lanes.data: a new object, catalogue, search or survey; branches toward a side only when its authors draw that conclusion
_lanes.future: a search that is running or planned, and what it could settle

entries.org: Gemini Observatory · Carnegie Institution for Science
entries.headline: 2012 VP113: a second Sedna
entries.text: A body several hundred kilometres across that never comes closer to the Sun than 80 AU. Only Sedna had been seen on such a detached orbit before.

branch.label: First to see the pattern
branch.text: The authors point out that the most distant objects all come closest to the Sun at a similar angle, and suggest an unseen super-Earth could be holding them there.

entries.org: Penn State · NASA's WISE all-sky infrared survey
entries.headline: Nothing big is hiding nearby
entries.text: An all-sky infrared search for a distant companion to the Sun by its parallactic motion, down to W2 = 14.5. Planet Nine, a few Earth masses and far fainter, is below its reach.
entries.stat: No Saturn analog within 28,000 AU; no Jupiter analog within 82,000 AU.

entries.headline: The founding paper
entries.text: Six distant objects share an orbital orientation. In simulations, a planet of roughly ten Earth masses on a wide orbit pointing the opposite way reproduces the pattern. They call it Planet Nine.

figure.alt: Batygin and Brown's diagram of the six orbits and the proposed planet

photos.commons: File:Konstantin Batygin by Christopher Michel in 2022 01.jpg

entries.org: Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur · Paris Observatory
entries.headline: Saturn's position narrows the hiding places
entries.text: Cassini's radio ranging to Saturn is precise enough that a massive planet in some directions would already have shown up as a tug. Those directions are crossed off; others stay open.

entries.who: Renu Malhotra, Kathryn Volk & Xianyu Wang
entries.headline: The orbits beat in simple ratios
entries.text: The orbital periods of the four most distant objects sit close to whole-number ratios of one period, as if locked in resonance with an unseen planet near 665 AU. A different argument that lands in the same place.

entries.who: Cory Shankman, JJ Kavelaars, Michele Bannister & the OSSOS team
entries.headline: Maybe we only found them where we looked
entries.text: A survey that recorded exactly where it pointed and how deep it saw finds striking, non-intuitive biases in which distant orbits get detected at all. Its own eight distant objects are consistent with orbits spread evenly around the sky.

entries.who: Juliette Becker & the Dark Energy Survey collaboration
entries.org: University of Michigan · Blanco 4-metre telescope, Chile
entries.headline: 2015 BP519: an orbit tilted 54 degrees
entries.text: Found at 55 AU on an orbit tilted 54 degrees out of the plane of the planets: by one measure the most extreme object then known.

branch.label: Circumstantial evidence
branch.text: The authors judge that it adds to the case for a planet: it would be the first of a predicted population of tilted, shepherded orbits.

photos.alt: The Víctor M. Blanco 4-metre telescope under the Milky Way

entries.headline: No planet required
entries.text: A swarm of small, distant bodies with enough combined mass can tilt and align itself through its own gravity. The clustering becomes a collective effect, not the work of one hidden world.

entries.who: Mike Brown, Konstantin Batygin, Fred Adams & Juliette Becker
entries.headline: One in 500, after the biases
entries.text: Modelling how the known surveys could have shaped the sample, the clustering still comes out about 1-in-500 unlikely by chance. A long review the same year shrinks the planet to 5 to 10 Earth masses on a somewhat closer orbit.

entries.org: University of Michigan · DES, OSSOS and the Sheppard–Trujillo survey
entries.headline: Three surveys, no significant clustering
entries.text: Pooling three surveys with published pointing histories and depths, the orientations of 14 distant objects are consistent with being spread evenly around the sky. The sample, they conclude, provides no evidence for clustering.

entries.headline: A map of where to look
entries.text: A redone bias analysis keeps the clustering significant at 99.6%, and a full orbital fit lands on a planet of about 6 Earth masses, closer and brighter than first proposed: around 380 AU out, a target a large telescope could find.

photos.commons: File:Konstantin Batygin by Christopher Michel in 2022 01.jpg

entries.who: Sigurd Naess & the Atacama Cosmology Telescope collaboration
entries.headline: Listening for its warmth
entries.text: A cold planet gives off its own faint heat. A blind millimetre-wave search of 18,000 square degrees finds no clear signal and leaves ten weak candidates for follow-up.

excluded.text: of the parameter space ruled out for a 5 Earth-mass planet (9% for 10 Earth masses)

photos.credit: The original uploader was Ahincks at English Wikipedia.

entries.headline: ZTF: nothing to V = 20.5
entries.text: A direct search of the Zwicky Transient Facility archive finds no candidate. The planet's own proponents start crossing off the sky.

excluded.text: of the predicted parameter space ruled out

entries.who: Mike Brown, Matthew Holman & Konstantin Batygin
entries.headline: Pan-STARRS1: most of the predicted planets are gone
entries.text: Pan-STARRS1 finds nothing to a depth of V = 21.5. What remains is faint and near where the Milky Way's plane crosses the ecliptic.

excluded.text: of the predicted parameter space now ruled out, with ZTF and DES

entries.who: Terry Long Phan, Tomotsugu Goto & colleagues
entries.org: National Tsing Hua University, Taiwan · IRAS and AKARI
entries.headline: One infrared candidate, 23 years apart
entries.text: Comparing two far-infrared all-sky surveys taken 23 years apart turns up one source that moved the right amount for a planet 500 to 700 AU away.

branch.label: If it holds up
branch.text: The motion fits a planet of 7 to 17 Earth masses. Two detections cannot fix an orbit, so it stays a candidate until someone follows it up.

entries.who: Ying-Tung Chen & the FOSSIL survey team
entries.headline: Ammonite: a fourth Sedna-like orbit
entries.text: 2023 KQ14, found with the Subaru Telescope, never comes closer than 66 AU and is stable for 4.5 billion years. Only three such objects were known before it.

branch.label: Points the wrong way
branch.text: Its orbit does not line up with the other Sedna-like objects, and its stability favours a large hypothetical planet on a wider orbit (about 500 AU) rather than a closer one.

photos.alt: The Subaru Telescope on Mauna Kea

entries.who: Sihao Cheng, Jiaxuan Li & Eritas Yang
entries.headline: 2017 OF201: a dwarf planet on an 830 AU orbit
entries.text: Roughly 700 km across, with a perihelion at 45 AU, pinned down from 24 observations over 20 years.

branch.label: Outside the cluster
branch.text: Its longitude of perihelion lies outside the observed clustering, which the authors call a challenge to the dynamical evidence for Planet Nine.

entries.note: Posted May 2025; published in ApJ Letters in February 2026.

photos.alt: Fuld Hall, Institute for Advanced Study
photos.commons: File:2023-12-02 15 10 02 Front view of Fuld Hall at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, Mercer County, New Jersey.jpg

entries.headline: The survey that should settle it begins
entries.text: On the night of 29 June 2026, Rubin's ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time starts. By October its pipelines have already turned up 2026 ED138, a probable dwarf planet 600 to 1,500 km across, in images taken before the survey formally began.

links.label: SLAC: first dwarf planet candidate (27 Oct 2026)

figure.alt: Vera C. Rubin Observatory under the night sky
figure.commons: File:Vera C. Rubin Observatory, iotw2229a - Night Light.jpg

entries.org: Legacy Survey of Space and Time
entries.headline: Find it, or close most of the remaining space
entries.text: Brown & Batygin's 2021 fit puts most of the predicted brightness within reach of a single Rubin image, though the planned survey does not cover the whole predicted path. A planet would show up as a slow mover crossing successive images; a few years of data will either find one or empty most of the space that is left.

photos.alt: The LSST Camera arriving at Rubin Observatory
photos.commons: File:LSST Camera Arrives at Rubin Observatory (rubin-2024 0517 RUBIN CAMERA Bonin AR307394).jpg

entries.headline: A few deep images could end it
entries.text: The IRAS–AKARI candidate, and two more from AKARI alone, each need a handful of deep optical pointings along their predicted tracks to be confirmed or dismissed. The teams name DECam and Subaru's Hyper Suprime-Cam as the instruments for the job.

entries.headline: Hearing its warmth, not its reflection
entries.text: The Simons Observatory's large telescope saw first light in 2025 on the same Chilean plateau as ACT, with far more sensitivity. Repeating ACT's shift-and-stack search there would test for the planet's own heat, independent of how much sunlight it reflects.

photos.alt: The Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope

entries.headline: Every new orbit is a vote
entries.text: Rubin is predicted to find tens of thousands of trans-Neptunian objects, among them the rare distant ones this whole argument rests on. If the newcomers cluster, the case strengthens. If they scatter like Ammonite and 2017 OF201, it fades, planet or no planet.
